title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
The page belongs to Grothendieck's sketch of a motivic Galois theory over finite fields. Modern reading:

(1) Setup. Let q = p^n. M(q) is a subgroup of Q'(i)*, most likely the multiplicative group of algebraic numbers. It is the group of Weil q-numbers: algebraic numbers u, units away from p, with |σ(u)| = q^{w/2} for every complex embedding σ, for some integer weight w.
- M(q) is the character group of the (conjectural) motivic Galois group G(q) of the Tannakian category of motives over F_q. That category is semisimple and commutative under Tate plus standard conjectures.
- f_q ∈ G(q) is the Frobenius element, i.e. the image of the arithmetic Galois group of F_q.
- Dually, a Weil number u is the character 'eigenvalue of Frobenius'.

(2) Inclusions. M(q^m) ⊂ M(q) ⊂ M(p): a Weil q^m-number of weight w is a Weil q-number of weight mw. Also M(q)^m ⊂ M(q^m), since |u^m| = (q^m)^{w/2}. Hence M(q^m)^m ⊂ M(q)^m ⊂ M(q^m) ⊂ M(q).

(3) Structure. M(q) ≅ Z × M^0.
- The map to Z is the weight.
- The splitting is given by q^{1/2}, a Weil number of weight 1. He writes 'n pair', presumably so that q^{1/2} is a rational integer.
- M^0 is the group of weight-0 Weil numbers: units outside p with all conjugates of absolute value 1, equivalently u·ū = 1, written as v(u) + v_p(ū) = 0.

(4) Transition maps. Extending scalars from F_q to F_{q^m} gives G(q) ← G(q^m), with f_{q^m} ↦ (f_q)^m. The transposed map on characters is M(q) → M(q^m), u ↦ u^m.
- It is the identity on the Z factor and multiplication by m on M^0.
- Its kernel is μ_m (dual of Z/mZ).
- Its image is M(q)^m ⊇ M(q^m)^m, so the cokernel is killed by m. Hence the kernel/cokernel of the dual map of group schemes is killed by m.

(5) Component groups. The opening lines say the component group G/G^0 of G(q) is the profinite group dual to the torsion of M(q), i.e. the roots of unity. It has coordinates in the dual of Ẑ, essentially Ẑ(1)-like.

(6) Passage to F_p-bar. He forms the inductive limit M(q^∞) = colim_q M(q) along u ↦ u^m, 'un groupe sans précédent', whose dual should be the motivic Galois group over F_p-bar.
- Since multiplication maps kill torsion, the limit is Z × (M^0 ⊗ Q)-like and torsion-free.
- So the group over F_p-bar is a connected pro-torus: the component group disappears.

This is exactly the Weil-number pro-torus P(q) and its limit P = lim P(p^n), with character group W(p^∞), later appearing in Langlands–Rapoport (1987) and Milne's 'Motives over finite fields' (1994), where the same notation W(p^∞) is used.
errors: The condition 'n pair' is not needed for the splitting M(q) ≅ Z × M^0: q^{1/2} is always a Weil q-number of weight 1 in the algebraic closure. It only matters if one wants q^{1/2} rational.

The condition 'v(u)+v_p(ū)=0' should be read as the global condition u·ū = 1 (equivalently all archimedean absolute values equal 1). Weight-0 Weil numbers are generally not p-adic units, so individual p-adic valuations need not vanish.
The description of the limit is unfinished. The colimit along multiplication maps kills torsion and tensors the weight-0 part with Q, which is not stated explicitly.
Everything presupposes the Tate and standard conjectures (semisimplicity, commutativity of the motivic group over F_q); this is left implicit.

ideas.what: Character group of the motivic Galois group of motives over F_q equals the group of Weil q-numbers, with Frobenius as a canonical element
ideas.modern_name: Weil-number protorus P(q) / motivic Galois group over a finite field
ideas.usually_credited_to: Langlands–Rapoport (1987); Milne (1994); ideas also in Saavedra Rivano (1972), Deligne–Milne
ideas.where_published: unsure; possibly echoed in Saavedra's thesis via Grothendieck

ideas.what: Splitting M(q) ≅ Z × M^0 via the weight and q^{1/2}; transition maps u ↦ u^m acting as identity on Z and multiplication by m on M^0
ideas.modern_name: weight grading / weight cocharacter of the Weil-number torus

ideas.what: Component group of G(q) is dual to the roots of unity (Ẑ(1)-like); it disappears over F_p-bar
ideas.modern_name: π0 of P(q); connectedness of P over F_p-bar

ideas.what: Inductive limit M(q^∞) of the M(q), dual to the motivic Galois group over F_p-bar
ideas.modern_name: W(p^∞), character group of the pseudo-motivic/Weil-number protorus P

missed.claim: Grothendieck (notes dated 1965 or the 1970s) already identifies the character group of the motivic Galois group over F_q with Weil q-numbers. He computes its structure Z × M^0, the transition maps, and the component group, and introduces the limit M(q^∞) for F_p-bar. This anticipates the Weil-number protorus P of Langlands–Rapoport and Milne, even in notation.
missed.quote: Considérons la limite inductive des M(q) (q variant multiplicativement) ... M(q^∞), un groupe sans précédent
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical credit: the Weil-number torus is central to the Langlands–Rapoport conjecture and the theory of motives over finite fields. It is usually attributed to Langlands–Rapoport/Milne, with only a vague nod to Grothendieck's Tannakian ideas.

deep.surprise_reason: A clear, explicit early computation of the motivic Galois group over F_q and F_p-bar as the Weil-number group, with transition maps, component group and the limit M(q^∞). This predates its standard attribution. The mathematics is elementary and Grothendieck's influence on the subject is generally acknowledged, so it is notable mainly historically.
transcription_corrections: 'Q'(i)*' is probably Grothendieck's notation for the multiplicative group of algebraic numbers (Q-bar*), not a literal field Q'(i).
'M^0 formé des u ∈ Q'(i)* ... unités dans ...' likely reads: units outside p, i.e. weight-zero Weil numbers.
'élévation à la puissance m' (labelled arrow) is confirmed by context: the map is u ↦ u^m.
'le noyau est le noyau de torsion plus (dual de Z/mZ)' should be read as: the kernel is μ_m, the m-torsion, dual of Z/mZ.
The marginal note ends: 'les transitions sur les M(q) sont l'identité sur Z et la multiplication par m sur M^0'.
